question: What is the normal resting heart rate for a healthy adult?
explanation: A resting rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute is the standard physiological range for healthy adults. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which structure acts as the primary natural pacemaker of the heart?
explanation: The sinoatrial node generates electrical impulses spontaneously to set the normal pace of the heart. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h1)

question: How does the vagus nerve affect the heart rate?
explanation: Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine, which has a parasympathetic calming effect that decreases the heart rate. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which neurotransmitter mediates sympathetic acceleration of the heart?
explanation: Norepinephrine is released by sympathetic nerve endings to stimulate beta-1 receptors on the heart, increasing rate and force. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h2)

question: At what threshold is a resting adult heart rate classified as tachycardia?
explanation: Tachycardia is formally defined as a resting heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute in adults. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why can a heart rate that is way too fast (severe tachycardia) become dangerous?

options.A: It leaves too little time for ventricular filling
options.B: It causes ventricles to empty too completely
options.C: It permanently damages the sinoatrial node
options.D: It stops all electrical activity in the atria

explanation: When the heart beats too fast, the chambers don't get enough time to fill with blood before pumping again. This means less blood goes out to the body! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h3)

question: Where is the best spot on the chest to listen to the apical pulse?

options.A: Third intercostal space at the right midclavicular line
options.B: Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
options.C: Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
options.D: Second intercostal space at the right sternal border

explanation: The apex of the heart rests near the fifth intercostal space on the left midclavicular line. That's your sweet spot for hearing the heartbeat clearly with a stethoscope! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h4)

question: What does a 'pulse deficit' mean when assessing a patient's heart?

options.A: The patient is experiencing severe hypothermia
options.B: Blood pressure cuffs were applied too loosely
options.C: Some ventricular contractions fail to produce peripheral pulses
options.D: The radial pulse is higher than the apical pulse

explanation: A pulse deficit happens when the heartbeat is too weak to create a strong pulse all the way down at the wrist. So, if you listen at the chest and feel the wrist at the same time, the chest count will be higher than the wrist count! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why does having a high fever usually cause your heart rate to go up (tachycardia)?

options.A: It directly cools the sinoatrial node tissue
options.B: It decreases circulating levels of epinephrine
options.C: It causes immediate failure of the vagus nerve
options.D: It increases the metabolic demand of body tissues

explanation: Think of fever as your body running on high gear. Your cells need more oxygen and energy when they're hot, so your heart has to pump faster to keep up with the demand. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which electrolyte imbalance is most commonly linked with a dangerously slow heart rate (bradycardia)?
explanation: Too much potassium in the blood (hyperkalemia) messes with the electrical signals in the heart muscle, which can slow things down and cause bradycardia. Balance is key! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the go-to emergency medication given for a patient with symptomatic bradycardia (dangerously low heart rate)?
explanation: Atropine is a trusty drug that blocks the vagus nerve, quickly giving the heart permission to speed back up to a safe rate. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h6)

question: As a nurse, why is finding the root cause of an abnormal heart rate just as important as treating the number itself?

options.A: Medications work better when the exact cause remains unknown
options.B: Treating the symptom without addressing the cause leaves the patient at risk
options.C: Doctors prohibit treating heart rates without laboratory confirmation
options.D: Monitors cannot display accurate rates unless the disease is cured

explanation: A weird heart rate is just a warning light on a car dashboard. If you only fix the gauge and ignore the engine smoking under the hood, your patient is still in serious danger! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is a major heart danger of having severe tachycardia for too long?

options.A: Excessive accumulation of blood in peripheral veins
options.B: Sudden permanent paralysis of skeletal muscles
options.D: Myocardial ischemia due to reduced coronary filling

explanation: The heart muscle feeds itself with blood while it rests between beats (diastole). When it beats too fast, it misses out on rest time, starving the heart of oxygen and causing ischemia. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h7)

question: Which clinical sign is a big warning flag for a sudden, severe drop in heart rate?
explanation: When the heart suddenly slows down too much, blood flow to the brain drops sharply. That's why patients often feel lightheaded or pass out completely (syncope). [learn more](GNS111_U2_T7#GNS111_U2_T7_h7)
